before.title: DIS Ignition Module / Coil Pack Failure Causing Cylinder Misfires
before.description: The Saturn S-Series uses a Distributorless Ignition System (DIS) with a waste-spark coil pack mounted on top of the engine. The coils and the Ignition Control Module (ICM) fail with age, throwing P0300-series misfire codes (commonly P0301 or P0302). A subtle but documented contributor is poor grounding: the ICM grounds to the transmission bellhousing via a stud, and corrosion on this ground path causes intermittent misfires that are easily misdiagnosed as coil failure. The waste-spark design uses the #4 plug firing on the compression stroke to fake a cam signal, so if the #4 coil weakens, the DIS may also lose its cam-position reference, causing cascading driveability issues.
before.solution: Diagnose by swapping the suspect coil with a known-good cylinder coil — if the misfire follows the coil, replace it. Before condemning the coil pack, inspect and clean the ICM-to-transmission ground stud: remove the bolt, wire-brush the contact surface on the transmission case down to bare metal, apply dielectric grease, and reinstall. Also clean and grease the ICM connectors. If grounds and coil swap don't fix it, replace the full coil pack assembly (~$80-150). Always replace the spark plugs and plug wires at the same time — the OE Champion plugs are specified for this engine; aftermarket platinum/iridium can cause its own misfires on the waste-spark system. Torque coil bolts carefully; the aluminum threads strip easily.
symptoms: Misfire DTC P0301, P0302, P0303, or P0304
Rough idle or shaking at idle
Hesitation or stumble on acceleration
Check Engine Light (often flashing under load)
Reduced fuel economy
Hard starting when warm

proposal.title: DIS Ignition Module / Coil Pack Failure Causing Cylinder Misfires
proposal.description: Saturn bulletin 97-T-30B addresses P0300 and P0301-P0304 on 1996-1997 S-Series DOHC LL0 vehicles and says misfires can come from ignition-secondary, mechanical, fuel or calibration conditions. The 1998-1999 factory diagnostic material does not identify coil or ignition-control-module failure as the universal cause; it uses crankshaft-velocity monitoring and component tests. The captured primary material does not establish age-driven coil/ICM failure across every frozen 1991-1999 engine, a corroded bellhousing ground as a model-wide defect, or the frozen number-four-plug/cam-reference cascade. Those claims and the parts-swapping prescription are removed.
proposal.solution: Record all DTCs, freeze-frame data and whether the MIL flashes, then identify whether the misfire is random, paired or cylinder-specific. Follow the year/engine diagnostic chart to test plugs, wires, coil secondary resistance/output, module power/grounds/connectors, fuel delivery, compression, leakage and calibration before replacing a component. Do not continue heavy-load driving with a flashing MIL. Do not buy a coil pack, ignition module, plugs or wires from this page; year, engine and measured ignition, fuel and mechanical results determine the repair, with no universal retail part.

before.title: EGR Valve Clogging Causing P0401/P0404/P1404 Codes
before.description: Beginning with OBD-II in 1996, the Saturn S-Series 1.9L EGR system is highly susceptible to carbon clogging. The narrow gap between the EGR pintle and its passage is easily fouled by exhaust carbon, especially on engines that burn oil (a chronic issue on this engine — see the oil consumption issue). The most common codes are P0401 (insufficient EGR flow), P0404 (EGR control circuit range/performance), and the Saturn-specific P1404 (EGR closed position). Replacing the valve alone rarely fixes the problem because the EGR passages in the cylinder head and intake manifold are also clogged. The condition worsens markedly once oil consumption begins.
before.solution: Remove the EGR valve and clean it: fill the valve body with carb cleaner, soak for 15 minutes, drain, and repeat 5-10 times. Use a T-handle Torx driver to manually work the pintle up and down to break free carbon deposits. Critically, also clean the EGR passages in the intake manifold and the supply tube/passage in the cylinder head — these are usually more clogged than the valve itself. A wire brush, pipe cleaners, and aerosol carb cleaner work well. If oil consumption is significant, expect the EGR to re-clog within 10,000-20,000 miles. Address oil consumption first for a lasting fix. Replacement EGR valves are inexpensive (~$50-80) but useless if the passages are not cleaned.
symptoms: Check Engine Light with code P0401, P0404, or P1404
Rough idle, especially after warm-up
Engine stumble on light acceleration
Stalling when coming to a stop
Failed emissions/smog test
Hesitation under light throttle

proposal.title: EGR Valve Clogging Causing P0401/P0404/P1404 Codes
proposal.description: Saturn bulletin 97-T-20A covers only 1996-1997 Saturn vehicles with P0401, P0404, P0405, P1404 or P1406 and says P1404/P1406 sensitivity can involve debris preventing the EGR pintle from seating. It requires updated diagnostic charts and, for identified PCM part numbers, a service calibration. The frozen page extends through 1999 and treats P0401, P0404 and P1404 as one carbon-clogging identity, but P0401 is a flow diagnosis while P0404/P1404 involve position/performance and can include circuits, valve movement, debris or calibration. The exact sources do not support the oil-consumption linkage, recurrence interval or claim that valve replacement rarely works.
proposal.solution: Scan all codes and capture commanded versus actual EGR position and operating conditions. For 1996-1997, identify the PCM part number and follow 97-T-20A before parts replacement or programming; for 1998-1999, use the exact model-year diagnostic charts. Inspect the connector, reference/feedback/control circuits, valve seating and flow path only as the chart directs. Do not soak the electrical valve body or force the pintle with an improvised tool. Do not buy an EGR valve, gasket, cleaner or PCM from this page; model year, DTC identity, PCM calibration and circuit/flow tests determine the repair, with no universal retail part.

before.title: Intake Manifold Gasket Coolant Leak at Cylinder #4 (DOHC 1.9L)
before.description: The 1.9L DOHC engine in the Saturn S-Series suffers from an intake manifold gasket failure where the OE one-piece gasket experiences compression set in the coolant passage between the manifold and the cylinder head, specifically at cylinder #4. Coolant leaks externally during cold-engine operation, sometimes evaporating before pooling on the ground, leading to mysterious coolant loss. A Saturn TSB documents the issue and the redesigned fix: a two-piece gasket consisting of a shorter orange intake manifold seal plus a separate black coolant seal made of a different elastomer. Most failures appear after 60,000 miles. The plastic intake manifold itself is also prone to broken coolant nipples.
before.solution: Replace the OE one-piece intake manifold gasket with Saturn's revised two-piece design (orange intake gasket + separate black coolant seal). Removal of the intake manifold also gives access to inspect and replace the brittle plastic coolant nipples that protrude from the manifold — these commonly snap off during service. Use new manifold bolts torqued to spec in the proper sequence. Total job is about 2-3 hours of labor. Always pressure-test the cooling system after the repair to verify the seal. While the intake is off, this is also a good time to clean the EGR passages, which are typically clogged on these engines.
symptoms: Coolant loss with no obvious puddle
Sweet coolant smell after cold start
Visible coolant residue near cylinder #4 intake port
Slight overheating during long drives
Steam from engine bay during warm-up
Low coolant warning despite recent top-off

proposal.title: Intake Manifold Gasket Coolant Leak at Cylinder #4 (DOHC 1.9L)
proposal.description: Saturn bulletin 01-T-15A directly documents an external cold-engine coolant leak behind the number-four intake port, but only 2000-2001 S-Series vehicles with the DOHC LL0 engine through VIN 1Z305500. It specifies a separate black coolant seal and shortened orange intake gasket after leak evidence is observed at that exact joint. The frozen page instead lists 1995-1999 and includes SOHC L24/LK0-style engine scope, so its indexed vehicle identity does not match the bulletin at all. The bulletin also does not support a 60,000-mile failure point, brittle plastic nipples across the frozen population, automatic new bolts or EGR cleaning while open.
proposal.solution: Pressure-test the cooling system cold and inspect the cylinder-head-to-intake-manifold joint behind the number-four intake port. Verify the vehicle is a 2000-2001 DOHC LL0 within the bulletin VIN range before using 01-T-15A; vehicles in the frozen 1995-1999 identity require their own leak diagnosis because that bulletin does not apply. Do not buy an intake gasket, coolant seal, manifold, pipe or bolts from this page; VIN, engine and the observed leak location determine the correct repair, with no universal retail part.
symptoms: Cold-engine external coolant stain at the exact number-four intake-port joint
Low-coolant warning or loss confirmed by pressure test
Overheating requiring immediate safe shutdown and diagnosis
Frozen 1995-1999 vehicle falls outside bulletin 01-T-15A
affectedSystems: DOHC LL0 intake-manifold coolant passage, exact bulletin only
Cooling system leak paths requiring separate diagnosis
